statements.label: A
statements.text: Ineffective triggering in COPD is caused by PEEPi acting as an elastic threshold load; the inspiratory effort must first overcome PEEPi before alveolar pressure can fall to the trigger level

statements.label: B
statements.text: Flow triggering is inferior to pressure triggering in patients with COPD and dynamic hyperinflation because it is more susceptible to auto-triggering from cardiac oscillations

statements.label: C
statements.text: Triggering delay in COPD — the time lag between neural inspiration onset and ventilator trigger — directly reflects the presence and magnitude of PEEPi

statements.label: D
statements.text: Applying external PEEP equal to 120% of measured PEEPi is recommended to eliminate all ineffective efforts in flow-limited COPD patients on pressure support

questions.explanation: Ineffective triggering and triggering delay are both caused by PEEPi's elastic threshold effect — the patient must reduce alveolar pressure by the full amount of PEEPi before the trigger threshold is reached. Flow triggering is preferred over pressure triggering in COPD because it detects the onset of inspiratory effort with less pressure change required (lower WOB per trigger), and is not inferior — it is actually less susceptible to auto-triggering from large Pes swings in severe DH. Triggering delay is a direct bedside measure of PEEPi magnitude. External PEEP at 120% of PEEPi would exceed the PEEP absorber threshold in flow-limited patients and would increase EELV in non-flow-limited regions — the consensus is 80%, not 120%.

questions.section: Part IV: Ventilatory Support and Mechanics
questions.question: Regarding assisted ventilation strategies to improve patient-ventilator synchrony in COPD:

statements.label: A
statements.text: High levels of pressure support (>20 cmH2O) are recommended in COPD to maximally unload inspiratory muscles, because higher support levels reduce PEEPi by decreasing inspiratory effort

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ineffective triggering can be reduced by applying external PEEP and by reducing PEEPi through bronchodilators and lower minute ventilation — these address the underlying mechanism

statements.label: C
statements.text: Maintaining spontaneous inspiratory effort during assisted ventilation, rather than converting to controlled ventilation, helps preserve respiratory muscle strength and diaphragm function

statements.label: D
statements.text: High PaO2 levels (>9 kPa/70 mmHg) are recommended in assisted ventilation of COPD to prevent hypoxic tissue injury, as the risk of oxygen-induced CO2 retention does not apply to ventilated patients

questions.explanation: External PEEP and PEEPi reduction through bronchodilators/minute ventilation reduction target the root cause of ineffective triggering and are the primary strategies for improving synchrony. High pressure support levels may paradoxically worsen hyperinflation by increasing tidal volume and shortening expiratory time — the increased intrinsic PEEP further worsens trigger problems. Maintaining spontaneous effort preserves diaphragm function and avoids rapid-onset disuse atrophy from paralysis or controlled ventilation. In assisted ventilation of COPD, high PaO2 (>9 kPa) should be avoided — it can lead to CO2 retention through the same Haldane and dead-space mechanisms that apply in non-ventilated patients; this risk persists during mechanical ventilation and was explicitly noted in the module.

questions.section: Part IV: Ventilatory Support and Mechanics
questions.question: Regarding external PEEP in assisted ventilation of COPD with dynamic hyperinflation:

statements.label: A
statements.text: The mechanism by which external PEEP reduces trigger work in flow-limited patients is by increasing expiratory driving pressure and forcing more complete lung emptying before the next breath

statements.label: B
statements.text: In COPD patients with expiratory flow limitation on assisted ventilation, external PEEP up to approximately 80% of PEEPi reduces inspiratory trigger work without increasing EELV

statements.label: C
statements.text: External PEEP also benefits patients without EFL on assisted ventilation by counterbalancing PEEPi and directly reducing the trigger threshold without any risk

statements.label: D
statements.text: Applying external PEEP in EFL patients narrows the alveolar-to-mouth pressure difference at end-expiration; the remaining PEEPi threshold to be overcome by the inspiratory muscles is approximately 20% of the measured PEEPi

questions.explanation: In flow-limited patients, external PEEP up to ~80% of PEEPi does NOT reduce trigger work by increasing expiratory flow — the flow ceiling from airway collapse means additional driving pressure cannot increase flow. Instead, the mechanism is that external PEEP raises the pressure at the airway opening, narrowing the gap between alveolar pressure (fixed at PEEPi by flow limitation) and mouth pressure, reducing the inspiratory effort needed to trigger. This is fundamentally different from a non-EFL mechanism. In patients without EFL, external PEEP increases EELV and worsens hyperinflation — it does not benefit these patients and carries risk. After applying 80% of PEEPi externally, the remaining trigger threshold is approximately 20% of the original PEEPi.

questions.section: Part IV: Ventilatory Support and Mechanics
questions.question: Regarding trigger mode selection in mechanically ventilated patients with COPD and dynamic hyperinflation:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pressure triggering is preferred over flow triggering in COPD with dynamic hyperinflation because the higher threshold reduces auto-triggering from cardiac oscillations

statements.label: B
statements.text: Flow triggering allows earlier detection of inspiratory effort with less patient work required to cross the trigger threshold, which is beneficial in the presence of PEEPi

statements.label: C
statements.text: Setting trigger sensitivity to maximum (lowest threshold) is sufficient to eliminate ineffective triggering even when significant PEEPi is present, making PEEPi reduction unnecessary in patients on pressure support

statements.label: D
statements.text: Maximising trigger sensitivity requires careful clinical titration to avoid auto-triggering, but it is not contraindicated — it can substantially reduce trigger work for patients with high PEEPi

questions.explanation: Flow triggering is preferred over pressure triggering in COPD patients with DH because: (1) flow changes at the airway opening are detectable with smaller changes in pressure than required for pressure triggering, reducing the work to cross the trigger threshold; (2) flow triggering does not require the full system pressure drop that pressure triggering demands. Maximising trigger sensitivity (lowering the threshold as much as possible without auto-triggering) is recommended to minimise inspiratory work. The concern about auto-triggering does not mean sensitivity maximisation is contraindicated — it means careful clinical titration is required. Auto-triggering from cardiac oscillations can occur at very high sensitivity settings but is not inevitable with careful adjustment in all patients.

questions.section: Part V: Supportive Therapies and Complications
questions.question: Regarding inhaled bronchodilator therapy during mechanical ventilation in COPD and asthma:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Both pMDI with spacer and nebulisers can effectively deliver bronchodilators to ventilated patients; efficiency depends on device positioning, particle size, and airway obstruction severity

statements.label: B
statements.text: The duration of bronchodilator effect in mechanically ventilated patients is typically 4–6 hours, identical to ambulatory patients, allowing the same dosing intervals

statements.label: C
statements.text: There is extensive evidence that inhaled beta-2 agonists administered via nebuliser or pMDI during invasive MV significantly decrease inspiratory resistance during both controlled and assisted ventilation modes

statements.label: D
statements.text: Inhaled corticosteroids carry the same level of evidence as systemic corticosteroids and are considered standard therapy in mechanically ventilated COPD patients

questions.explanation: Both pMDI-with-spacer (connected to the inspiratory limb) and nebulisers effectively deliver bronchodilators in ventilated patients, with efficiency influenced by technique, particle size, and obstruction severity. The duration of bronchodilation in ventilated patients is shorter — 90–180 minutes — not the 4–6 hours typical in ambulatory use; more frequent dosing may be required. Multiple physiological studies confirm that inhaled bronchodilators during MV significantly reduce inspiratory resistance in both controlled and assisted modes. Inhaled corticosteroids, in contrast, have insufficient evidence during MV and are not considered standard therapy alongside systemic corticosteroids in this setting.

questions.section: Part V: Supportive Therapies and Complications
questions.question: Regarding heliox therapy in mechanically ventilated patients with obstructive lung disease:

statements.label: A
statements.text: The lower gas density of heliox (70–80% He/20–30% O2) reduces turbulent flow resistance in central airways, potentially decreasing work of breathing and PEEPi

statements.label: B
statements.text: Heliox is equally effective at all FiO2 levels because helium viscosity — not density — is the primary determinant of flow resistance benefit

statements.label: C
statements.text: Heliox may cause significant discrepancies between set and delivered tidal volumes because standard ventilator flow meters are calibrated for air/oxygen mixtures

statements.label: D
statements.text: Sufficient evidence exists to make heliox a first-line recommendation for all mechanically ventilated patients with severe COPD or asthma

questions.explanation: Heliox reduces turbulent airflow resistance by substituting the low-density helium for nitrogen, reducing Reynolds number in central airways. Its benefit is density-dependent, not primarily viscosity-dependent — as FiO2 increases and helium fraction falls, gas density approaches that of air and the benefit is lost. This is the core limitation in hypoxaemic patients. The flow meter discrepancy (calibrated for air/oxygen) causes clinically important set vs. delivered VT differences requiring careful monitoring. Despite promising physiological effects, evidence for heliox in mechanically ventilated COPD and asthma remains insufficient and conflicting — it is not a first-line recommendation and is reserved for patients with mild hypoxemia unresponsive to standard therapy.

questions.section: Part V: Supportive Therapies and Complications
questions.question: Regarding complications of mechanical ventilation in COPD and asthma:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Mechanically ventilated COPD patients have the highest incidence of barotrauma among all respiratory failure aetiologies because of dynamic hyperinflation and high peak pressures

statements.label: B
statements.text: VAP occurs in 10–27% of all mechanically ventilated patients; COPD independently increases VAP risk by approximately 2.35-fold compared with non-COPD ventilated patients

statements.label: C
statements.text: In COPD patients with high Ppeak but low Pplat (e.g. Ppeak 50, Pplat 24 cmH2O), barotrauma risk is primarily determined by Ppeak rather than Pplat

statements.label: D
statements.text: Non-fermenting gram-negative bacilli, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, are the predominant VAP pathogens in COPD patients — even in early-onset VAP cases

questions.explanation: Despite theoretical risk from DH, early studies show COPD patients have the lowest barotrauma incidence among respiratory failure aetiologies — not the highest. VAP epidemiology: 10–27% of all ventilated patients, with COPD conferring 2.35× excess risk. Barotrauma risk is determined by Pplat (alveolar distension pressure), not Ppeak — a high Ppeak with low Pplat reflects high airway resistance without dangerous alveolar distension. Non-fermenting gram-negative bacilli dominate COPD-related VAP pathogen profiles, even in early-onset cases, which is a key distinction from community-acquired pneumonia patterns and should inform empiric antibiotic selection.

questions.section: Part V: Supportive Therapies and Complications
questions.question: Regarding intensive care unit acquired weakness (ICUAW) in mechanically ventilated COPD and asthma patients:

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reported incidence of ICUAW in patients ventilated for more than 7 days is 25–60%, encompassing both polyneuropathy and myopathy

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 30% incidence of critical illness myopathy from combined NMBAs and corticosteroids in severe asthma applies equally to stable COPD patients who have not received NMBAs

statements.label: C
statements.text: The primary treatment for ICUAW once established is complete respiratory muscle rest using controlled ventilation to prevent further injury from patient inspiratory effort

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pre-existing nutritional deficits, low BMI, and respiratory cachexia in COPD are disease-specific factors that contribute to higher ICUAW risk beyond the general ICU population baseline

questions.explanation: ICUAW incidence of 25–60% after >7 days MV is well-established. The 30% CIM incidence with combined NMBAs and corticosteroids in severe asthma cohort studies is a specific drug combination warning. COPD patients have disease-specific ICUAW risk factors beyond generic ICU illness: low BMI, respiratory cachexia, frequent corticosteroid use, and frequent NMBA exposure. These are not shared by all ICU patients. Paradoxically, the treatment for ICUAW is NOT complete respiratory muscle rest — this causes diaphragmatic atrophy. Management includes early mobilisation, maintaining spontaneous breathing efforts (assisted ventilation preferred over controlled), limiting NMBAs and corticosteroids, glycaemic control, and neuromuscular rehabilitation.

questions.section: Part V: Supportive Therapies and Complications
questions.question: Regarding long-term outcomes and prognosis in mechanically ventilated COPD patients:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Long-term prognosis for mechanically ventilated COPD patients is influenced by pre-morbid functional status, nutritional state, and comorbidities

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reported 6-month mortality rate for mechanically ventilated COPD ranges from 5–15%, similar to outcomes following ICU admission for community-acquired pneumonia

statements.label: C
statements.text: The majority of patients with severe acute asthma who require invasive mechanical ventilation have a favourable long-term lung function prognosis, as MV itself does not worsen long-term asthma outcomes

statements.label: D
statements.text: Five-year survival rates following MV for AECOPD approach 80–90% when cardiovascular comorbidities are aggressively managed with evidence-based therapies

questions.explanation: Pre-morbid functional status, nutritional state, comorbidities, and prior exacerbation history all influence long-term prognosis after MV for AECOPD — factors that clinicians should consider before deciding on ventilatory support. Six-month mortality ranges from 40–70% across studies (not 5–15%), substantially worse than most other ICU respiratory failure aetiologies. In contrast, acute asthma requiring MV does not per se worsen long-term asthma prognosis — the long-term outlook in asthma depends on longitudinal lung function changes from airway inflammation, not on the acute episode. Five-year survival after MV for AECOPD may approach 10% (mortality ~90%) — not 80–90% survival.

questions.section: Part V: Supportive Therapies and Complications
questions.question: Regarding supportive therapies and nutritional support in mechanically ventilated COPD and asthma patients:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Overfeeding mechanically ventilated COPD patients — particularly with high-carbohydrate nutrition — increases CO2 production, raising the minute ventilation requirement and potentially impeding weaning

statements.label: B
statements.text: Early enteral nutrition is not recommended in mechanically ventilated COPD patients because impaired gastric motility from high PEEP creates prohibitive aspiration risk

statements.label: C
statements.text: Patients with COPD who are critically ill typically have pre-existing nutritional deficits; early enteral nutritional support is recommended to meet their increased metabolic demands

statements.label: D
statements.text: Hypovolaemia at the time of intubation in patients with COPD is unusual; hypotension after intubation more commonly results from cardiac dysfunction and should be managed with vasopressors rather than fluid resuscitation

questions.explanation: Overfeeding with high-carbohydrate nutrition significantly increases CO2 production (RQ=1.0 for carbohydrates) and ventilatory requirements, potentially preventing successful weaning in patients near the ventilatory threshold — a well-established principle in COPD management. Early enteral nutrition is recommended for critically ill COPD patients (not contraindicated); aspiration risk requires appropriate precautions (head-of-bed elevation, gastric monitoring) but does not justify withholding enteral nutrition. COPD patients often have severe pre-existing nutritional deficits from increased energy expenditure and reduced intake. Hypovolaemia at intubation in COPD is in fact common — patients are often severely dyspnoeic for days with limited fluid intake and high insensible losses; post-intubation hypotension may relate to both DH and hypovolaemia and often benefits from fluid resuscitation alongside DH management.
